display: Social worker who coordinates a sewing circle for refugee women in Western Sydney.

signals.text: The sewing circle has outgrown its host's lounge room: more women than machines, and someone is always standing.
Two new members joined recently, and I want to keep welcoming people without turning anyone away.
I need a weekday-morning space with power points for about six machines, because school hours are the only time the women are free.
The women want to take small alteration orders (hems, zips, school uniforms) to earn some money, and I don't yet know how to set that up.
I'd like a way for the women to find paying neighbours for alterations, with fair pay and no charity framing.
I need an overlocker (or a way to get one), because alterations don't work without finished edges.
The overlocker we borrow has to go back in about three weeks, and our petty cash is $63 against a $480 second-hand machine.
I've emailed three councils and a church about space and got kind replies but no keys. A hall at $38 an hour is out of reach, and the next grant round isn't until February.
I'm anxious about rent and housemates after my housemate moves out at the end of October.
I sometimes feel that my social work degree only counts for something because of this circle, and I'm worried about leaning that hard on it.
I'm stretched across a part-time legal centre job, volunteer firefighter training, the circle and a wedding in March, and I'm often tired.
I'm planning a $6,000 wedding in Penrith and making my own dress, so I'm looking for ideas and favours that keep costs down.
My family doesn't see the circle as real work, and I'd like examples that show it has value.

offers.text: Four years of casework with newly arrived families, and a social work degree.
I run a sewing circle of about nine regular members, meeting twice a week, with two years of track record.
Working relationships with a settlement services agency, a council community development officer and two churches.
A group of skilled hand and machine sewers, some of them former professional dressmakers, who do careful hemming, zips and alterations.
I can coordinate a small paid-work pilot, covering fair pricing, scheduling and quality checks, as a coordinator who knows the women's availability.
I can run culturally careful, mixed-language sessions using pictures, demonstration, basic Dari and a laminated picture dictionary of pattern-making terms.
I can share a template for starting a small community sewing group: how to set it up, how to run it, and a dictionary of visual terms.
The circle can cater small events, with fair payment for the women. Home-style cooking is available.
Volunteer firefighter training, with basic emergency preparedness skills.
Twelve months of grant-funded fabric, thread and needles, which I can use to run a trial with a partner.

catchers.hypo: Hi, I manage a church hall (or a community room) that sits empty on weekday mornings. Could a group use it?
catchers.can: I can bring a regular weekday-morning group of about nine to eleven women with their own machines, who need power points and a few tables, and who would look after the space.
catchers.confirm: Is the space free on at least two weekday mornings a week, between school drop-off and pick-up, with power outlets for several machines?

catchers.hypo: I'm replacing my overlocker and have an old one in the cupboard. Do you know anyone who could use it?
catchers.can: The circle needs an overlocker for its alteration work. I can collect it, arrange a thank-you and make sure it gets used by the women.
catchers.confirm: Is the machine in working order, and can it be lent or given for a community group?

catchers.hypo: I own a tailor shop, or work in fashion, and I'd like to give some practical help to women who sew skilfully.
catchers.can: I can connect you with the circle for mentoring on professional alteration standards, pricing and customer handling.
catchers.confirm: Are you willing to give a few hours of hands-on practical advice for free, without taking over the women's decisions or payments?

catchers.hypo: Our council or housing body wants to support refugee-led micro-enterprise but doesn't know where to start.
catchers.can: I can pilot an alteration service with women who have the skill and the demand, and I know the council contacts and what blocks them.
catchers.confirm: Can you fund or arrange a venue and a machine, rather than offering only advice or a grant that covers fabric?

catchers.hypo: I run a small business, school or sports club in Western Sydney and need uniform repairs or alterations done regularly.
catchers.can: The circle can take a regular batch of alteration work at fair rates, and I will coordinate pickup, turnaround and quality.
catchers.confirm: Do you have a steady volume of hems, repairs or alterations, and are you willing to pay a fair price rather than donate?

catchers.hypo: I'm a social worker or youth worker starting a similar craft group for newly arrived women and want to learn from someone who has done it.
catchers.can: I can walk you through starting up, running a group in more than one language, and the pitfalls of space and funding.
catchers.confirm: Are you planning to run an ongoing, participant-led group rather than a one-off workshop?

catchers.hypo: I'm a grants writer or fundraiser and I'd like to volunteer a little time for a community group.
catchers.can: I can use your help on an application for venue and equipment funding, ahead of the February round.
catchers.confirm: Do you have experience with small local-government or foundation grants for venue and equipment costs?

catchers.hypo: I'm Tessa's friend of a friend, looking for a room in a shared house in Sydney from November.
catchers.can: A housemate is moving out in late October, so I can talk to someone about the room.
catchers.confirm: Are you looking for a shared house in Western Sydney from late October, and comfortable with sewing machines in the living space?

catchers.hypo: My mother used to sew professionally and now lives alone. She would love to meet other women who sew.
catchers.can: I can introduce her to the circle through a friend of the family, if she is happy to join in on her own terms.
catchers.confirm: Does she speak enough English, or another language the group shares, and can she get to Blacktown on weekday mornings?

forbids.text: I won't share the women's immigration histories, their family details or any personal case information.
I won't present the women as objects of charity. If they do paid work, it must be paid fairly.
The women can only meet on weekday mornings, so evening or weekend schedules don't work for them.
I can't take on anything that needs a venue budget, because the grant covers fabric and thread only.
I'm limited on weekends by firefighter training and rostered days, and by a part-time job on weekdays.
I won't make the women's stories or photos public for fundraising or publicity without their own consent.

projects.name: Western Sydney sewing circle
projects.text: A twice-weekly sewing circle for refugee women in Blacktown that has outgrown its lounge room.

projects.name: Alteration pilot
projects.text: A small paid alteration service run by the women for neighbours, covering hems, zips and school uniforms, with fair pricing.

policy.t1: Circle size, the shortage of space and equipment, the weekday-morning venue need with power for about six machines, the alteration idea, and what the grant covers.

policy.never: The women's immigration histories, any family members' names, and any personal case details.
